title: What the Bible Actually Says About Anxiety
excerpt: Worry is not a wiring problem. It is a tell. And it tells the truth about what we are leaning on — which is exactly why Matthew 6 does not say try harder.
body:
Most people who struggle with anxiety can name the hour. For a lot of them it sits somewhere around three in the morning. The house is quiet. The people they love are asleep. And they are awake, working through the same short list they worked through last night and will work through again tomorrow night. Nothing gets solved at that hour. They know nothing is getting solved. They cannot stop anyway.

We tend to treat that hour as a malfunction, a glitch in the machine. We come at our own fear the way a mechanic comes at a car that will not start. Find the broken part. Replace it. Move on. The right book, the right breathing exercise, the right verse on the mirror, and we could solder it shut and sleep like the calm people we assume everyone else to be.

But anxiety is not a broken part. Anxiety is a tell.

It tells the truth about what we are actually leaning on. People do not lie awake over the things they have genuinely handed to someone stronger than themselves. They lie awake over the things they believe, at three in the morning, depend entirely on them. Follow your worry down far enough and it leads, nearly every time, to a place where you have quietly concluded, without ever deciding it on purpose, that you are the one holding everything up, and that if you let go, it falls.

The word the New Testament uses for worry is *merimna*. It shows up on the lips of Jesus in the most famous passage ever spoken about anxiety, the sixth chapter of Matthew, and it is older and stranger than our English softens it into. *Merimna* carries the sense of being divided, pulled apart, drawn in two directions at once. The anxious person is not someone with too much on their mind. The anxious person is someone being torn — the heart pulled toward the God it half-trusts and toward the future it cannot control, stretched between them until something begins to tear.

That is what three in the morning is. The sound of a soul being pulled in two.

There is a detail we tend to skim. When Jesus says "do not be anxious" in Matthew 6:25, he opens with a word that should stop us: *Therefore.* It is a conclusion. He is drawing a line from what he said one verse earlier: "you cannot serve God and money." The anxiety teaching is not a fresh subject. It is the second half of the money teaching. Worry, it turns out, is what serving the wrong master feels like from the inside. It is the tax the false master charges, payable nightly.

Then he does something genuinely strange. He does not say try harder. He does not say think positively. He points out the window. *Look at the birds.* The sparrows that never planted a field or filled a barn, and are fed anyway. Then the sentence the whole passage turns on, the one we skim because we have heard it so often: *Are you not of more value than they?*

He is not insulting your intelligence. He is rebuilding your trust from the foundation up. He takes the person who is convinced, at three in the morning, that they are alone and in charge and holding up the sky, and walks them back out into a created world that is fed, every day, by a hand that is not theirs.

I want to be careful here, because the church has done real damage at exactly this point. To tell a person whose chest tightens at a full inbox, whose hands shake before the phone rings, to "just have more faith" is not the gospel. It is a slap with a Bible verse on it. Some people carry anxiety the way a soldier carries shrapnel, lodged deep, from a wound they did not choose. *Consider the Birds* talks plainly about the body, the doctor, and the medication, and treats all three as good. I am not going to stand at a safe distance and call your trembling a failure of belief.

But I will not pretend it is only chemistry, either. Because that is the other lie, the gentler one, and it abandons you just as surely. It tells you your fear means nothing. And in the comfort of that, it takes away the one thing that could heal you — the possibility that your restlessness is pointing somewhere. That it is a hunger. And that hungers can be fed.

That is what *Consider the Birds* is about. It is for the person awake at three in the morning, and it does not promise the hour will never come again. What it promises is that the hour does not have to mean what you have been afraid it means.

The birds are singing this morning. They started before it was light.

title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
excerpt: The Bible's first concern about money is not how much you have. It is what it is doing to you. Jesus named it mammon and treated it as a rival master.
body:
Jesus talked about money more than he talked about heaven, and far more than he talked about hell. By a common reckoning, about one of every ten verses in the Gospels touches it, and roughly a third of his parables turn on it. He came to deal with sin and death, and he spent a striking share of a short public life talking about what people earn, keep, owe, and fear losing.

We have quietly agreed not to notice.

Money is the one subject a congregation will forgive a pastor for nearly anything except raising. We will sit still for hard preaching on pride, on anger, on doubt. Bring up money and the room changes temperature. That reaction is worth paying attention to, because we do not guard what does not matter to us. We guard what we are afraid to lose. The flinch is information.

Here is the question the Bible actually asks, and it is not the one we expect. Its main concern about money is not how much you have. It is not even, first, what you do with it. It is what it is doing to you.

Because money, in the teaching of Jesus, is never only a tool. He says something about it he says about nothing else. He gives it a name and treats it as a rival. "You cannot serve God and money" — and the word he used was *mammon*, an Aramaic word he personifies, a master with a throne and a claim. He never does this with sex. He never does this with power. Only money gets named as a rival god, because money, more than almost anything we handle, has the strange ability to stop being something we own and start being something that owns us.

I want to be careful, because the church has gone wrong here in two opposite directions. One made God a means to money: give, and he will make you rich. That is mammon in a clerical collar. The other made money itself the sin, so that a paid-off house or a good meal becomes a failure of holiness. That is a different lie. The Bible does neither. It does not flatter wealth, and it does not romanticize poverty. It tells the truth about a power, and it offers to set us free.

And it tells that truth to all of us, which is the part we resist. We assume the warnings are for the rich, by which we always mean someone richer than we are. The man with the boat aims the verse at the man with the yacht. Everyone has someone above them to point it at, so it never lands. But mammon does not check your balance before it goes to work on you. The pull is the same in a trailer and a penthouse.

Here is the line that holds everything together: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." Read it slowly, because the order is not what we assume. We think the heart leads and the money follows — that we fund what we already love. Jesus says it runs the other way. The treasure leads, and the heart follows it, the way a compass needle turns north whether or not you meant it to.

That is either very bad news or very good, depending on what you do with it. It means you cannot simply decide to care less about money by trying harder. But it also means there is a door. Move the treasure, and the heart will follow it out.

That is the hope underneath the whole thing, and it is not a technique for getting rich or a guilt trip for being comfortable. It is freedom. The closed fist — gripping, calculating, never quite able to rest because the number is never quite enough — can become an open hand. Not by willpower. Not by shame. By the slow, real work of moving our treasure to a place that cannot be lost, until the heart, that obedient compass, finally turns and follows it home.

You cannot serve both. That is not a threat. It is a mercy.

title: Cast Your Anxiety on God: The Violent Verb We Turned Soft
excerpt: We hear "cast all your anxiety on him" as a gentle invitation to relax. The Greek is a word for hurling. The casting is an act of the will, not a feeling — and you do it before the peace arrives.
body:
The most important word in the most quoted verse about anxiety is a verb of violence, and we have turned it into a verb of feeling.

"Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). We have heard it as an invitation to relax — to let go, gently, the way you release a held breath. But the Greek word is *epiripsantes*, and it is not gentle. It is the word for hurling, flinging, throwing something off of yourself with force. It appears in only one other place in the New Testament — Luke 19:35, when the disciples *threw* their cloaks onto the colt for Jesus to ride into Jerusalem. They did not drape them. They flung them. Peter is not telling the anxious to unclench by mood. He is telling them to take the whole crushing load of it and *throw* it — bodily, deliberately, with their will — onto Someone else.

This matters more than it seems, because it tells us anxiety is not finally cured by understanding. You can grasp every argument, see the sparrow clearly, and still lie awake, because insight is not the same as the act. There is a moment, every time, when the trembling soul has to actually do something with the weight in its hands. Throw it. And the throwing is an act of the will that does not wait for the feeling to arrive first. This is the great mistake of the anxious Christian — waiting to *feel* peaceful enough to let go, when the order runs the other way. You cast first. The peace comes after, often much later, sometimes not until you have cast the same worry a hundred times. The casting is the obedience. The peace is the fruit.

But you cannot throw a weight into empty space. Peter does not say cast your anxiety into the void. He says cast it *on him.* And then he gives the reason, and the reason is the entire foundation: *because he cares for you.* The Greek is even more intimate — *because it matters to him concerning you.* The casting is only possible because of the catching.

And we have torn apart what Peter wrote as one sentence. "Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God... casting all your anxieties on him." Casting is the participle of humbling. They are the same act. We think of our anxiety as the opposite of pride — it feels like weakness, like smallness. But Peter sees underneath it. To insist on carrying what God has offered to carry is to insist that you are the one who must hold it. The white-knuckle grip is not humility. It is the last refuge of a pride that will not bow.

Here is the part nobody tells you: you will have to cast the same anxiety over and over. You will throw it onto God tonight and find it back in your own hands by morning, and you will have to throw it again. This is not failure. This is the life of faith. The casting is a muscle. It is weak at first. It gets stronger only by being used.

So here is the shape of it, as concretely as I can give it, because abstractions do not help at three in the morning. Name it — the actual specific fear, out loud if you can. Humble yourself — bow, get under the hand of God, confess that you cannot carry this and were never meant to. Cast — hand the named thing to God in plain words. And then leave it. Do not pick it back up to inspect it. When you find it back in your hands, do not despair. Throw it again. Name, humble, cast, leave. Repeat for the rest of your life.

A thoughtful person is raising the objection: *this sounds like a trick I play on myself.* It is a fair challenge, and the answer is the center of the Christian claim. The casting is not a trick of the mind, because the One you are casting on is not a figment of the mind. If the tomb is really empty, if the Father who fed the birds is really there, then casting is not a mental exercise at all. It is the most realistic thing you can do.

The anxious clutching is the fantasy. The casting is the realism. We have them exactly backwards. The clutcher is living in a fantasy where he is god and alone. The caster is living in the real world, where he is small and kept.

title: You Cannot Serve God and Money: What Jesus Meant by Mammon
excerpt: Jesus did not call money a tool. He gave it a name — mammon — and set it opposite God as a rival lord. "Money" is a thing you manage. Mammon is something that manages you.
body:
The verse most of us know — that no one can serve two masters — was not spoken to misers. Jesus said it on a hillside to ordinary people who carried the same mixture of ordinary ambition and ordinary worry that fills a congregation on any Sunday. The rival master he names is not an extreme case. It is the ordinary case.

He calls it mammon.

"No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24). Read it line by line. "No one can serve two masters." The Greek is *douleuō*, the slave word — not an employee who divides a shift between two jobs, but a slave, with a single lord whose claim is total. An employee can work for two employers. A slave cannot. The verse does not ask whether you find money demanding. It asks who holds the title to your life. The point is not that serving two masters is difficult. It is that it is structurally impossible. Someone holds the title, even if the slave does not know it yet.

"You cannot serve God and mammon." *Mammon* is Aramaic, and in Jesus' day it was the everyday, unremarkable word for your stuff — possessions, property, wealth. Jesus did not reach for a specialized term of rebuke. He reached for the ordinary word and turned it into a name. In verse 24, money is not a tool or a resource. It is a *kurios* — a lord, a master, set grammatically parallel to God, a rival for the same position. Jesus is not saying money can become a distraction. He is saying money occupies the same category as God. It makes a claim on the heart. It offers security, identity, status, a future. Those are not the functions of a tool. They are the functions of a lord.

The early church found the word striking enough to leave untranslated. Jerome kept *mammon* in the Latin Vulgate rather than converting it to *pecunia*. The King James kept it in 1611. Only in the twentieth century did versions begin rendering it simply "money" — a choice that gains clarity and loses the personification in the same stroke. "Money" is a thing you manage. Mammon is something that manages you.

Tim Keller, in *Counterfeit Gods* (2009), called money "the most versatile" idol, because it can stand in for nearly every other — success, control, approval. And he says what the church has been slow to say: the idol of money is not primarily the problem of the very wealthy. It is the problem of anyone who trusts money to do what only God can do. The person anxious about financial security, who cannot imagine giving freely because the future feels too uncertain, is not miserly. They are afraid, and they are using money as the wall they have built against the fear. The wall is the idol. It does not have to be a very large wall.

Jacques Ellul, in *Money and Power* (1954), pressed further: money is a genuine spiritual power, and it has an agenda. It is not content to be held and used. It moves toward ownership. The person who thinks they are using money is being slowly transformed by it. None of this feels like worship. It feels like good sense. That is how a spiritual power works — not through dramatic temptation but through the gradual normalization of its logic, until its values are simply how we think.

Here is what the passage will not let us avoid. When we hear "you cannot serve God and mammon," we instinctively locate the target across the room — the extravagant spender, the aggressive accumulator, the one with more than us. But the verse gives us no exit. It addresses everyone who has two potential masters, and unless you are entirely without money, you have two. The rebuke belongs to us before it belongs to anyone else.

So what breaks the grip? Not less desire. Idols are not destroyed by removal — the heart immediately finds a replacement. They are displaced by a greater love. Jesus does not simply tell us to give money away. He tells us we cannot serve two masters, and then he shows us a better treasure. The open hand is not an absence of desire. It belongs to a person who has found something to hold that does not require the fist. The generous person is not someone who wants less. They are someone who has found more.
